Our proposed metrics concentrate evaluation of forecasts to a focus region, representing high-utility or distributional tails, by collapsing the body of the distribution to a single pivot. Our benchmarks on time-series foundation models (TSFMs) reveal that while a clear ranking can be formed for distribution capture, there is no clear winner for tasks like systemic load prediction. This indicates that models with a strong ability to capture an overall distribution do not produce forecasts with high downstream utility. To encourage the use of the proposed metrics we open-source the efficient signature kernel (ESK) library. This library facilitates batch computation, with custom triton kernels, achieving a speed-up of up to 3.58$\times$ compared to implementations via the popular SigKernel library. Code for our metrics are available on GitHub.

items.title: Defining equations for two-block shallow ReLU pattern varieties
items.summary: We give a complete algebraic characterization of two-block shallow ReLU pattern varieties. We show that the determinantal equations arising from rank constraints imposed by the activation patterns generate the defining ideals, thereby proving a conjecture of Alexandr-Montúfar. The set-theoretic proof uses a characterization of orbit closures of matrix pencils in terms of the Kronecker canonical form.

items.title: Sensor Monitoring Towards Industry 4.0: Bridging Concepts on the $C_n$ Multivariate Control Chart
items.summary: The main challenge in monitoring multiple sensors is the high dimensionality that a process can easily reach. From a decision-making perspective, converting these multivariate dynamics into an informative visualization is also not trivial. Statistical Process Control (SPC) techniques detect changes in quality characteristics, but they are difficult to apply beyond the normality (Gaussian) assumption. For instance, the most well-known SPC multivariate control chart is based on Hotelling's $T^2$ statistic, which assumes that the process data follow a multivariate normal distribution (which rarely occurs in practice) and that the observations are serially independent. This study focuses on the multivariate case (dimension $d \geq 2$), regardless of the data dependence or marginal asymmetry. We propose a new control chart for change detection in copula-based multivariate processes, called the $C_n$-chart, which is based on a density level-set tolerance region built from a copula function, and we derive its run-length properties. The methodology also quantifies the (not necessarily linear) dependence among the variables. Two case studies are presented, one on water quality control and the other on monitoring brass-steel thermostats, complemented by a simulation study of run-length performance and computational cost. The results show that the proposed methodology captures both the association among variables and the anomalies, and that it accommodates variable selection through conditional (regression) modeling of the margins.

items.title: CAFE-AQI: Coverage-Aware Day-Ahead AQI Forecasting with Early Warning and Conformal Uncertainty in Bangladesh
items.summary: Next-day air quality forecasting often assumes city records are equally complete and independent. However, an audit of a large Bangladesh dataset revealed a sharp coverage expansion after August 2022 and showed that 103 city labels correspond to only 61 unique AQI trajectories. To address these issues, this paper presents CAFE-AQI, a coverage-aware framework for forecasting next-day maximum AQI. It also estimates the probability of Unhealthy-or-worse conditions (AQI >= 151). Data were divided chronologically into training (2022-2023), calibration (2024), and testing (2025). To prevent duplicate records from dominating training and evaluation, identical trajectories were weighted. The framework combines temporal and pollutant features with a five-neighbor spatial context. It also includes a class-balanced warning head and risk-conditional conformal calibration aimed at providing early warnings and prediction intervals. Evaluation on the duplicate-balanced 2025 data gave an MAE of 9.76, an RMSE of 15.04, and an R-squared value of 0.910 for CAFE-AQI. Its MAE was 3.63 AQI lower than persistence (95% CI: 3.49-3.76), with lower errors in each of the 61 trajectory groups. For unhealthy-air warnings, the F1-score was 0.908 and the AUROC was 0.982. The nominal 90% intervals covered 92.09% of observations. When an entire spatial block was excluded from training, the MAE remained 10.66, showing that the lightweight model transferred reasonably well to unseen locations.

items.title: Improved Leverage Score Sampling for Constrained Active Linear Regression
items.summary: In this paper we study active learning for constrained linear regression. Given a design matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, a constraint set $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, and query access to $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we seek an approximate solution to $\min_{x\in C}\|Ax-b\|_2^2$ using as few queries as possible. This problem arises in many scientific and engineering applications, and randomized leverage score sampling provides a powerful method to solve it. However, existing leverage score methods ignore the constraint or encode it through ridge regularization, suffering unfavorable query complexity for anisotropic constraint sets. We propose ellipsoid-regularized leverage scores, where we approximate the constraint set by an outer ellipsoid and use its shape matrix to bias sampling toward directions that matter under the constraint geometry. We prove that the query complexity is governed by an anisotropic effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}(C)\le d$. With appropriate parameters, $O(d_{\text{eff}}(C)\log d/\varepsilon^2)$ queries suffice to return a point in $C$ with objective value at most $(1+\varepsilon)$ times the optimum. This bound can substantially improve on the standard leverage-score bound, since anisotropic constraints can make $d_{\text{eff}}(C)$ much smaller than $d$. For convex constraints, we improve the dependence on $\varepsilon$ from $1/\varepsilon^2$ to $1/\varepsilon$. We also prove two lower bounds: first, the $d/\varepsilon^2$ dependence is unavoidable without convexity assumptions on $C$, and second, in some regimes, the effective dimension dependence $d_{\mathrm{eff}}(C)/\varepsilon$ is necessary for ellipsoidal constraints. Experiments on synthetic regression problems and a parametric heat conduction problem show lower regression error than standard baselines for similar query budget.

items.title: Risk-optimal active learning with informative abstention
items.summary: We study label acquisition when an oracle may abstain and its response probability shares parameters with the classifier. A query can then provide information through both a returned label and the response outcome. Under a correctly specified parametric model, we derive the classifier information after adjustment for response-model nuisance parameters. Combining this information with the local curvature of multiclass zero-one risk gives an acquisition criterion for minimizing the leading asymptotic excess risk. We characterize the optimal allocation under a fixed query budget and show how query allocation affects response identifiability. The oracle criterion reduces to response-discounted acquisition when response probability does not depend on the classifier parameters. Simulations examine the resulting query allocations and isolate the contribution of the response-outcome term through an ablation. A Consumer Complaints replay retains observed human abstentions and reveals benchmark labels upon response. Response-aware acquisition has lower mean test error than response-discounted acquisition at the two largest budgets, with paired differences significant after Holm correction. Entropy sampling performs better at the smallest budget. The gains depend on the response mechanism and query budget.

items.title: Developing a Subdistrict-Level Economic Progress Index Using Geospatial Data
items.summary: This paper develops an Economic Progress Index (EPI), a composite measure built from Earth Observation (EO) and open geospatial data with unsupervised Principal Component Analysis (PCA) weighting. The index captures the observable productive and enabling capacity of local economies and the intensity with which economic space is used. Sub-national monitoring in developing economies is held back by sparse data: district GDP estimates arrive with multi-year lags, rely on price deflators and top-down allocation, and do not exist at the subdistrict (taluka/tehsil) scale where place-based policy is targeted. The EPI fuses multi-sensor satellite data, gridded population and OpenStreetMap road and amenity networks across 357 subdistricts of Maharashtra, India, over 46 quarters (2015 Q1 - 2026 Q2). Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS (STL) separates long-run trends from monsoon and crop-cycle seasonality. A non-negative PCA gives sign-consistent, interpretable weights and rankings nearly identical to standard PCA ($ρ$ = 0.998). Across districts, the index explains 74% of the variation in the NFHS-5 wealth index, 52% in household consumption (HCES 2023-24) and about 78% in real district GDP levels (65% in logs), but does not track short-run output growth. Because it measures structural capacity rather than annual output, the index kept rising through the FY2020-21 COVID-19 contraction. Across Maharashtra's six revenue divisions, relative inequality fell by 44% even as the absolute gap between leading and lagging divisions widened by 32%; district-level $β$-convergence implies a half-life of about 14 years. The framework offers a scalable, deflator-free basis for structural monitoring in data-sparse economies.

items.title: A Matching Lower Bound for Online Smooth Calibration
items.summary: We study smooth calibration error in sequential binary prediction, a measure of how far probabilistic forecasts are from being calibrated that is robust to small perturbations of the forecasts. The minimax smooth calibration error is known to lie between $Ω(T^{1/3})$ and $O(\sqrt T)$(Qiao and Zheng, 2024), where $T$ is the number of rounds. We close this gap for both adaptive and oblivious adversaries. We construct an adaptive adversary whose outcome mean moves with the forecaster's cumulative residual, which makes compensating for past residuals costly and forces every forecaster to incur $Ω(\sqrt T)$ expected smooth calibration error. Simulating this adversary against the forecaster's average prediction yields an oblivious adversary with the same guarantee. These lower bounds match the known $O(\sqrt T)$ upper bound up to universal constants, and are therefore minimax optimal. Our results also imply matching $Θ(\sqrt T)$ bounds for calibration distance and lower calibration distance. The proof ideas are partially developed by GPT-6 Astra under the authors' guidance.

items.title: Variable Length Diffuse Everything: Arbitrary Length Generative Modeling on Arbitrary State Spaces
items.summary: Diffusion and flow-based generative models have achieved remarkable results across diverse applications, but most assume data of fixed-dimension/length. Meanwhile, real-world problems such as layout generation often involve variable-length, multimodal data, such as continuous bounding box coordinates paired with discrete types. Existing methods typically address variable length by padding data to a fixed size or by introducing specialized objectives to model lengths explicitly, adding complexity and limiting generality. We propose Variable Length Diffuse Everything (VL-DE), a simple and general framework for variable-length multimodal generation on arbitrary state spaces. Instead of padding, VL-DE handles variable length through an insertion-based mechanism grounded in a principled theoretical framework, yielding a tractable training objective. In addition, by utilizing the fact that VL-DE is based on a generator with an additive form, we develop a higher-order sampler by appropriately handling the time dependence. Extensive experiments on layout and molecule generation demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

items.title: A Multisite Super Learner for Survival Prediction with Limited Target-Site Data
items.summary: Survival prediction models developed in multi-site studies may transport poorly to a new site because of between-site heterogeneity in covariate effects and baseline hazards. Pooled models may fail to capture site-specific risk patterns, while site-specific models can be unstable in small cohorts. We propose a Multi-Site Super Learner (MSSL), a domain-adaptive ensemble for survival prediction that combines diverse pooled and site-specific base learners. A meta-learner optimizes the ensemble weights using source data alone or, if available, a small target-site calibration sample. In simulations, when even a small target-site sample was available, MSSL substantially reduced prediction error relative to a pooled super learner under moderate to large between-site heterogeneity and generally matched or improved upon models fit to the target-site data alone. It did so by downweighting dissimilar or noisy models and upweighting models from structurally similar sites. Without target-site data, MSSL did not improve upon the pooled super learner. In an application to predicting dementia progression using the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) Uniform Data Set across 10 sites, MSSL matched or outperformed standard super learning using pooled data in 9 of 10 sites. MSSL offers a practical framework for adapting multi-site survival prediction models to a new site when a small calibration sample is available.

items.title: A Free Lunch: Gradient Averaging Achieves Optimal Statistical Efficiency in Newton Sketch
items.summary: We study statistical inference for online sketched Newton methods, in which each Newton system is approximately solved by an inner randomized sketching solver. Existing work reveals a computational--statistical trade-off: the sketching solver (and its accelerated variants) reduces the per-step cost of Newton methods from $O(d^3)$ to $O(d^2)$, but the randomness introduced by sketching also inflates the limiting covariance of both the last and the averaged Newton iterates. In this work, we address this trade-off via gradient averaging. We show that simply replacing the stochastic gradient with a moving average at each step can mitigate, and in some cases eliminate, the trade-off in Newton sketch. Importantly, gradient averaging requires no additional oracle evaluations and leaves the contraction bound of the inner sketching solver unchanged. In particular, we prove that the last sketched Newton iterate with gradient averaging attains a limiting covariance no larger than that without gradient averaging, while the averaged iterate even attains the minimax optimal limiting covariance, matching that of the exact Newton method. To our knowledge, this is the first analysis showing that randomness introduced to improve computational efficiency need not compromise statistical efficiency as long as proper gradient estimates are used. The key analytical challenge is that gradient averaging destroys the crucial martingale difference structure underlying central limit theorem arguments. We overcome this challenge by analyzing the coupled two-timescale recursions governing the iterate and the gradient estimator. Numerical experiments on linear and logistic regression support our theoretical covariance comparisons.

items.title: Randomization protects the average, not the trial: chance covariate imbalance and a calibration of balance $P$ values at the design stage
items.summary: Randomization makes the unadjusted treatment-effect estimate unbiased over the allocations a scheme could produce, although it does not balance any single trial. Chance imbalances on strongly prognostic baseline variables directly threaten the validity and regulatory credibility of trial results, yet what design-stage balance $P$ values imply for bias and error rates is seldom stated. We review evidence on chance covariate imbalance and derive that link under a linear model with one normal prognostic covariate, with simulation checks. Given the realized allocation, the unadjusted estimate is biased by $β$ times the difference in covariate means; in standard-error units the bias is $ρZ_{\mathrm{bal}}$, where $ρ$ is the covariate-outcome correlation and $Z_{\mathrm{bal}}$ the balance z-statistic, so it does not shrink as trials grow. Pre-specified ANCOVA removes this bias, change scores reverse it, and non-collapsibility attenuates odds and hazard ratios even under perfect balance. A worst-balance threshold of $P = 1/e$ marks where the Sellke-Bayarri-Berger bound reaches 1; under complete randomization the worst of $k$ independent balance $P$ values falls below it with probability $1-(1-1/e)^k$, 0.99 for $k=10$. Any balance $P$ value $\geq 0.317$ keeps the two-sided conditional type I error of the unadjusted test at or below 5% for every $ρ$; at $1/e$ the one-sided error in the favoured direction is at most 4.1%, against 13-33% at $P = 0.05$. Design-stage balance scores should be benchmarked against complete randomization, weighted by external prognostic strength, and reported alongside allocation predictability and a pre-specified covariate-adjusted analysis plan.

items.title: When Do LLMs Model the Right Target? Problem Formulation in High-Stakes Risk Prediction
items.summary: Generative AI is increasingly used to assist with data science tasks, yet fundamental questions remain about its ability to correctly formulate analytical problems. We investigate how well large language models (LLMs) can formulate prediction problems when developing models for high-stakes decision making. We focus on one particular challenge to validity: decision dependency, which arises when historical decisions affect observed outcomes. We evaluate this aspect of problem formulation in LLM-generated code and explanations across child-welfare, healthcare, and employment settings, using 11 models from OpenAI and Anthropic and seven prompt conditions. We assess whether the LLM-generated code implements a procedure appropriate for estimating the intended outcome under the study's assumptions and whether the explanation acknowledges decision dependency. We find that LLMs do not reliably address decision dependency without guidance in the prompt. When prompts specify the target, the assumption needed to estimate it, and the estimation procedure, target-aligned implementation reaches 99-100%. Among frontier models, a simple prompt description of how decisions affect outcomes appears sufficient to elicit target-aligned implementation. Some responses also acknowledge decision dependency without addressing it in their code. Our findings suggest that analysts should not rely on LLMs to correctly formulate prediction problems without explicit methodological guidance and careful review. We propose validity-centered guidelines for LLM-assisted predictive modeling, covering prompt formulation, validation of the target and estimation procedure, and identification of key assumptions. Establishing validity is a necessary early step in evaluating whether to deploy a predictive model in a high-stakes setting, but deployment requires weighing broader ethical, institutional, and practical considerations.

items.title: How Path Integral Diffusion Decides a Finite Spin Glass
items.summary: When an AI diffusion-type generator samples a frustrated spin glass, which macroscopic alternatives does it decide first, and when? We study this for bridge-diffusion models of the Path Integral Diffusion (PID) type started from a point source. We show that every isotropic PID is a time-changed Gaussian stochastic localization, and conversely every signal-to-noise schedule is realized by a PID protocol. What a continuous-time generator decides therefore does not depend on the protocol, which only sets when and at what cost. We describe the generator's state by its partial commitments: the probabilities it assigns, at each moment, to nested classes of configurations fixed by the target. The partial commitments are martingales that move only along class contrasts. Their ensemble average gives the information about each level at an exact rate set by squared magnetization contrasts. In the balanced, effectively binary approximation, a split reaches half of its class information near γ=1.044/λ_P, where λ_P is the leading eigenvalue of the parent covariance. The theory is applied to Bethe-lattice and Sherrington--Kirkpatrick (SK) glasses with up to 24 spins. It is observed generically that a trajectory first shifts its weight to one of the two mirror halves of the zero-field measure and then to the glassy classes inside it. These classes appear near the glass transition, keep their identity on cooling and are absent in a ferromagnet on the same graphs. Sparse (Bethe) and dense (SK) glasses differ in how often and how strongly such classes exist, not in how trajectories commit to them. For a generator that takes finitely many steps, the protocol matters through the late, local stage rather than the macroscopic decisions. Sampled posteriors at N=32,64 and small trained denoisers show the same sequence.

items.title: Efficient Variance-Aware Reinforcement Learning in Time-Inhomogeneous Linear MDPs
items.summary: We study variance-dependent reinforcement learning in episodic time-inhomogeneous linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with feature dimension $d$, horizon $H$, and $K$ episodes. While recent works have established variance-dependent regret with $\tilde{O}(1)$ deterministic-regime overhead for linear mixture MDPs (Zhao et al., 2023) and worst-case nearly minimax optimal regret $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K} + d^7 H^8)$ for linear MDPs (He et al., 2023),, existing variance-aware analyses for linear MDPs (Li and Sun, 2023; Huang et al., 2023) rely on a coarse concentration step whose resulting regret guarantees retain a polynomial $\tilde{O}(K^{1/4})$ additive term even in deterministic environments. We propose VA-LSVI-UCB++, a computationally efficient algorithm that achieves the variance-dependent regret bound $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H\min\{\mathrm{Var}_K^*,\mathrm{Var}_K^π\}}+d^5H^4)$, where $\mathrm{Var}_K^*$ and $\mathrm{Var}_K^π$ denote the cumulative conditional variances of the optimal value function and the played policies' value functions along the realized trajectory. Our result adapts to the minimum of the two realized trajectory variances, recovers the worst-case minimax optimal leading term $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K})$, and collapses to $\tilde{O}(d^5 H^4)$ in deterministic environments, free of polynomial-in-$K$ dependency. At the core of our analysis is a simultaneous three-way reference-advantage decomposition for the optimistic, pessimistic, and squared value function estimators coupled with variance self-bounding and Freedman-type value-difference arguments, which tightens the pessimistic and second-moment confidence radii by a factor of $\tilde{O}(d H)$ and removes the inverse-variance-floor blowup.

items.title: When Features Beat Noise: A Noise-Driven Hypothesis Testing Method for Feature Selection
items.summary: Feature selection has remained a daunting challenge in machine learning and artificial intelligence, where increasingly complex, high-dimensional datasets demand principled strategies for isolating the most informative predictors. Despite widespread adoption, many established techniques such as Boruta, Recursive Feature Elimination and other wrapper based methods suffer from notable limitations; some incur substantial computational cost, while others offer no definite statistical driven stopping criteria or assess the significance of their importance scores. This paper proposes a novel feature selection method that addresses these limitations. Our approach introduces multiple random noise features and evaluates each feature's importance against the maximum importance value among these noise features incorporating a non-parametric bootstrap-based hypothesis testing framework to establish a solid theoretical foundation. We establish the conceptual soundness of our approach through statistical derivations that articulate the principles guiding the design of our algorithm. To assess reliability and practical utility, we validated the method on controlled simulations and diverse real-world datasets, where it consistently outperformed established feature-selection approaches including Boruta, Model-X Knockoffs, RFE, LASSO, Elastic Net, and mRMR in recovering meaningful signals. Hence, the method emerges as a robust algorithm for principled feature selection, enabling the distillation of informative predictors that support reliable inference, enhanced predictive performance, and efficient computation.

items.title: Prescriptive Learning of Linear Policies with Feasibility Guarantees for Binary Decision-Making
items.summary: Binary decision-making under uncertainty arises across a wide range of applications, including energy systems scheduling, transportation, and workforce planning. While machine learning has been increasingly applied to accelerate or replace mixed-integer solvers in such settings, existing approaches rely on predictive learning, training models to reproduce optimal decisions from labeled data, which lacks knowledge of counterfactual outcomes and provides no guarantees that the resulting decisions will be feasible. This limitation is further compounded under distributional shift, where policies trained on historical data may produce systematically infeasible decisions. We propose a prescriptive learning framework for binary decision-making that addresses both limitations. Rather than predicting optimal labels, the framework jointly optimizes over linear decision policies and feasible assignments across all training scenarios, allowing feasible alternatives and their operational performance to be considered directly during training. We further extend the framework to a distributionally robust chance-constrained formulation using a Wasserstein ambiguity set, which enforces feasibility with a prescribed probability under the worst-case distribution in the ambiguity set and enables a tunable trade-off between robustness and solution quality. We demonstrate the framework on two case studies, namely a unit commitment problem and a staff allocation problem. Out-of-sample experiments under test distributions that either match or differ from the training distribution show that the robust model is more conservative when the two distributions coincide, while under distributional shift it substantially reduces unmet demand and lowers total cost by up to 76.5% relative to classical predictive learning.

items.title: Confounding Heterogeneity in Multivariate Sensitivity Analysis for Observational Studies
items.summary: In observational studies, unmeasured confounding may bias causal conclusions even after matching on measured confounders. Sensitivity analysis is therefore usually needed to assess the robustness of causal conclusions to unmeasured confounding. We consider multivariate sensitivity analysis that assesses the causal effect of a single treatment on multiple outcomes. We identify an inherent feature of such analyses, which we call ``confounding heterogeneity'': different outcomes may be affected by distinct unmeasured confounders, and a common unmeasured confounder may affect different outcomes to varying degrees. Building on matched observational studies, we formulate sensitivity analysis frameworks that accommodate confounding heterogeneity. We show that Type I error control for many existing sensitivity analysis methods is guaranteed under sensitivity analysis models and modes of inference that differ fundamentally from those used in the classic framework. We study asymptotic power using design sensitivity and Bahadur-Rosenbaum efficiency and examine finite-sample power through numerical studies. Our results show that the structure of unmeasured confounding affects sensitivity analysis, and that widely used single-parameter frameworks may mischaracterize the sensitivity of a causal conclusion to unmeasured confounding when confounding heterogeneity is considered. Simulations and a data application illustrate the practical importance of confounding heterogeneity in multivariate sensitivity analyses.

items.title: Instrument indeterminacy: separating uncertainty in POVM effects and its neutrosophic reading
items.summary: Neutrosophic annotation frameworks for quantum measurement attach an external triple $(t,i,f)$ to each Born probability, and explicitly leave open how indeterminacy could be defined operationally. We show that indeterminacy cannot be recovered from outcome probabilities, but can be computed from the pair (state, effect). For a binary POVM $\{A, I-A\}$ we define the instrument indeterminacy $\mathcal{I}_ρ(A) = 4 \mathrm{Tr}(ρ(A-A^2))$, which vanishes exactly when the state only sees the sharp part of the effect. The normalized Gini index of the outcome splits as $4TF = \mathcal{I}_ρ(A) + 4 \mathrm{Var}_ρ(A)$, a law of total variance that separates the instrument contribution from the state contribution; the identity is a special case of Massar's POVM uncertainty operator, and our contribution is its neutrosophic reading. Moving the system-apparatus cut to a Naimark dilation transfers exactly $\mathcal{I}_ρ(A)$ from indeterminacy to variance, which yields the missing operational definition. We extend the decomposition to $m$-outcome POVMs, relate the minimum indeterminacy of two incompatible unbiased qubit observables to their commutator through Busch's joint-measurability criterion, and show that $\mathcal{I}_ρ(A)$ equals twice the disagreement probability of a repeated Lüders measurement. The resulting estimator needs neither the state nor the effect and, in simulation, requires 2.5 to 6 times fewer shots than detector tomography for the same error.

items.title: Spatial Extremes on Domains with Physical Barriers
items.summary: We propose a model for spatial extremes what realistically accommodates nonconvex domains. Most existing models assume that tail dependence between locations depends only on their separation. Even if extended to be anisotropic or nonstationary, they still cannot accommodate features between points that may mediate the dependence. This assumption limits their applicability in settings where physical barriers like mountains, coastlines, or islands may attenuate or even block dependence in extreme events. In this work, we use the idea of a visibility graph to modify an existing spatial random scale model. This results in a tail dependence model that naturally accommodates nonconvex spatial domains, where the nonconvex features are interpreted as physical barriers. Furthermore, the model inherits key properties from the scale mixture like the ability to represent asymptotic independence at long ranges and either asymptotic dependence or asymptotic independence at short ranges. We apply our model to two applications in which physical barriers feature prominently in determining the spatial structure of extreme events. The first is precipitation in the South Island of New Zealand, where the Southern Alps shelter the eastern region from the effects of atmospheric rivers which arrive from the west. The second is significant wave heights in the North Atlantic, where the Faroe Islands tend to block the effects of extratropical cyclones traveling into the North Sea.

items.title: Efficient Causal Survival Inference under Limited Surrogate Monitoring
items.summary: Post-treatment surrogate endpoints can improve the efficiency of causal survival effect estimation, but their monitoring may end before follow-up for the primary outcome. We investigate the impact of limited recurrence monitoring on semiparametric efficiency when mortality follow-up continues. We derive the efficient influence function under limited monitoring and establish an exact expression for the efficiency gain from extending monitoring between any two durations. The resulting efficiency comparison characterizes when extending surrogate monitoring improves precision and distinguishes these gains from those available with a fully observed surrogate. We develop a doubly robust estimator under limited surrogate monitoring and establish asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency for its cross-fitted version under suitable conditions. Simulations and an application to breast cancer data illustrate the proposed method.

items.title: Pragmatic Curiosity: A Unified Framework for Hybrid Learning and Optimization via Active Inference
items.summary: Many engineering and scientific workflows rely on expensive black-box evaluations, requiring sequential decisions that must both improve task performance and reduce uncertainty. Bayesian optimization (BO) and Bayesian experimental design (BED) provide powerful but largely separate treatments of goal-directed optimization and information-seeking experimentation, leaving limited guidance for hybrid settings in which learning and optimization are intrinsically coupled. We propose Pragmatic Curiosity (PraC), a unified framework for hybrid learning and optimization via active inference. PraC evaluates candidate queries by trading information gain about a task-relevant latent symbol against an expected regret-based potential over outcomes. This formulation foregrounds three operational design choices: which latent quantity should be clarified, how task value is encoded as regret, and how strongly information gain should be exchanged against pragmatic regret. We instantiate PraC across three regimes of increasing complexity: decision-oriented monitoring with fixed global symbols and known downstream losses, targeted active search with induced local symbols and evolving coverage goals, and composite Bayesian optimization with hierarchical regret learning under unknown preferences. Across these regimes, PraC reduces downstream decision risk, improves coverage of critical outcome regions, and jointly learns predictive and preference structures without relying on task-specific staging rules.

items.title: Federated Differential Privacy with Batch Contamination
items.summary: We study mean estimation under federated differential privacy (FDP) constraints and batch contamination, considering both Gaussian and heavy-tailed distributions. In the homogeneous setting, where sample sizes and privacy budgets are constant across servers, we show that the costs of privacy and contamination disentangle. Under a bounded $v$th moment condition, with $v \in (1, \infty)$, the cost of batch contamination is of order $(\varepsilon/n)^{2-2/v}\vee \varepsilon^2/n$, where $\varepsilon$ is the contamination level and $n$ is the per-batch sample size. This reveals a phase transition at $\varepsilon\asymp n^{1-v/2}$, for $v > 2$, which is the first of its kind in the literature. We develop a two-stage procedure that achieves the minimax rate up to poly-logarithmic factors. A key component is a private smoothed voting procedure tailored to the FDP setting that provides optimal sensitivity control. For heterogeneous batch sample sizes and privacy budgets, we introduce a batch partitioning framework that groups batches with comparable per-batch sample sizes and privacy budgets. Surprisingly, the minimax rate is determined, up to poly-logarithmic factors, by the most informative group of batches. Consequently, in some regimes, it is minimax optimal to use only an arbitrarily small proportion of the data set. Heterogeneity also introduces interactions between the costs of privacy and contamination, in contrast to their disentanglement in the homogeneous setting. For unknown contamination level, we propose an adaptive, near-minimax optimal Lepski-type extension for the heterogeneous Gaussian setting, designed specifically to prevent privacy leakage by ensuring no repeated use of data points.

items.title: Bounded-Order Non-Identifiability in Latent Structure Block Models: The Fiber in Closed Form
items.summary: A graphon is determined by all of its homomorphism densities, but motif-based methods use finitely many. We compute exactly what that truncation costs in a natural family: latent structure block models whose positions lie on $K$ rays, equivalently degree-corrected block models of rank two. For a given radial law, the configurations that agree on every graph with fewer than $2K-1$ vertices form a one-dimensional fiber, which we give in closed form with explicit endpoints; the friendship graph $F_{K-1}$ is its unique edge-minimal separator, so no fixed motif order serves every $K$. The separating signal is suppressed by a factor of at most $m_1^{2(K-1)}$, where $m_1$ is the mean squared slope, about $10^{-4}$ at $K=4$: detecting it from motif counts would take about $10^{15}$ nodes in a single graph, at any edge density. The information is nonetheless in the graph; the fiber belongs to the statistic, not the model. Common spectral pipelines, which count no motifs, still slide along the fiber by more than a third of its length at ordinary densities, with confidence regions that almost never contain the truth, while model-based fits of the same embedding do not. We give practitioners four checks: whether a fit is at risk, what to run instead, why a confidence interval will not warn, and how wide the remaining ambiguity is.

items.title: Stability of Parallel Transport Convolution under Riemannian Metric Perturbations
items.summary: Geometric convolutions on Riemannian manifolds depend on the geometry of the underlying domain, making stability under metric perturbations a fundamental question in geometric deep learning. This paper studies this question for parallel transport convolution through methods from differential geometry and analysis. On a fixed compact manifold, we establish that, for a continuous input signal and a continuous reference kernel supported in a sufficiently small normal neighborhood, the convolution output depends continuously in $L^2$ on the Riemannian metric in the $C^2$-topology, under the specified localization and transport-path conventions. The analysis develops perturbation estimates for geodesics, parallel transport, Jacobi fields, and exponential maps, and uses these estimates to compare the transported kernels. A central difficulty is the cut locus, which obstructs uniform comparison of the transport construction over the entire manifold. We address this difficulty by combining uniform estimates away from the cut locus with integral bounds on neighborhoods of arbitrarily small volume, while also controlling the change in the Riemannian volume measure. The resulting qualitative stability theorem connects perturbation theory for Riemannian geometric constructions with the analysis of spatial convolution operators in geometric deep learning.

items.title: Balancing Partition Forest for Causal Weighting
items.summary: Balancing weights are used in observational causal inference to construct a population in which the treatment is independent of observed pretreatment covariates. The ideal weight is the ratio between the product of the covariate and treatment marginals and their joint distribution, for binary and continuous treatments alike. We propose Balancing Partition Tree (BPT) and Balancing Partition Forest (BPF), which estimate this ratio on a learned rectangular partition of covariate--treatment space. Each split maximizes the gain in a Bregman divergence computed from joint and marginal counts. Two choices of divergence yield criteria that maximize the mutual information captured by the partition or reduce the squared error of the weights. We show that the population residual of either criterion bounds the bias of inverse-probability-weighted and doubly robust response estimators that use the population partition weights. Across 17 synthetic and semi-synthetic settings and three response estimators, BPF obtains the lowest mean RMSE rank among seven weight estimators, and a single tree fits in 0.14 seconds on 16,512 observations.

items.title: Unsupervised dense random survival forests identify interpretable patient profiles with heterogeneous treatment benefit
items.summary: Precision oncology seeks to match patients with treatments that maximize clinical benefit. Identifying clinically interpretable subgroups with differential treatment effects from randomized clinical trials, however, remains challenging. We propose a subgroup-discovery framework based on dense random survival forests, with a splitting criterion that combines prognostic discrimination and treatment-effect heterogeneity. The framework aggregates patient proximity matrices across multiple forest configurations, identifies subgroups using the resulting treatment-informed similarity representation, and summarizes them through concise covariate rules. An empirical calibration procedure assesses evidence for treatment-effect heterogeneity. Extensive simulations demonstrate the ability of the framework to distinguish heterogeneous from homogeneous treatment-effect settings and recover treatment-responsive subgroups, with empirical Type I error control under the homogeneous scenarios considered. An application to a Phase III oncology trial identifies a treatment-responsive patient profile defined by baseline characteristics, illustrating the potential of the framework to inform subgroup-focused clinical research and future trial design.

items.title: Parameter-Specific Bias Diagnostics in Random-Effects Panel Data Models
items.summary: The Hausman specification test assesses the random-effects specification by comparing random-effects and fixed-effects estimators. This note uses the diagnostic of Karl and Zimmerman (2021) to give a coefficient-specific sensitivity summary from one fitted mixed model. The diagnostic measures alignment between fitted random effects and the weights used to estimate a coefficient or contrast. Its value need not equal finite-sample bias: fitted effects are shrunken, and response-dependent covariance estimates introduce an additional weighted-error term. We explain this distinction, describe simulations that refit the covariance parameters and retain the latent-effect and weighted-error contributions, and illustrate the calculations with gasoline-demand data and a multiple-membership value-added model. Connecting the diagnostic to established generalized least squares sensitivity analysis, including Vasnev's (2010) balanced-panel results, we identify it as the negative derivative of a coefficient or contrast with respect to the log scale of the random-effects covariance. With fitted covariance shapes held fixed, integrating the diagnostic over this log scale, upward from the fitted model, gives the random-effects estimate minus the fixed-effects estimate for a contrast estimable under both models. We also discuss conditioning on stochastic regressors and the additional assumptions needed for calibrated inference.

items.title: Laplace Bayesian transport maps for generative modeling of non-Gaussian climate fields
items.summary: Transport maps provide a powerful framework for the generative modeling of complex, non-Gaussian spatial fields, such as those encountered in climate science. By mapping a complicated target distribution to a standard Gaussian reference distribution, they can serve as efficient stochastic surrogates. However, current Bayesian transport maps, which are modeled using autoregressive Gaussian processes, typically rely on empirical Bayes estimates that ignore hyperparameter uncertainty. Here, we contrast this point-estimate approach with a fully Bayesian model that provides posterior uncertainty quantification in transport map hyperparameters. To avoid the high cost of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), we also propose a Laplace approximation to the hyperparameter posteriors, which can be computed at negligible additional computational cost relative to empirical Bayes. We provide numerical evidence and a real-data climate application demonstrating that these Laplace approximations can accurately capture most posterior summaries at a fraction of the cost of MCMC, while maintaining good predictive properties. Thus, our approach offers a scalable, uncertainty-aware framework for the generative modeling of non-Gaussian climate fields.

items.title: DL101 The Representation Capability of Neural Network Models
items.summary: Universal approximation theorems (Cybenko, Funahashi, Hornik & Leshno) provide the mathematical justification for why neural networks are powerful enough to model complex, nonlinear phenomena. Shallow networks can approximate any continuous function on compact sets. Leshno's theorem clarified that non-polynomial activations are necessary for universality, which explains why ReLU, logistic, hyperbolic tangent, and other common activations work (but pure polynomials do not). However, approximation theorems provide no efficiency, training, nor generalization guarantees. They do not indicate how many neurons are needed for a given accuracy, whether gradient descent will find the right parameters, or whether networks trained on finite data will generalize well. Barron provided quantitative error bounds for particular function classes (approximation rates for functions with bounded Fourier norm), whereas Montúfar was the first to show that expressivity grows exponentially with depth (in terms of the number of linear regions). Deep networks are strictly more expressive than shallow ones with the same number of parameters. Depth is fundamentally more powerful than width, providing a rigorous mathematical explanation for the use of deep learning models.

items.title: Wasserstein Target Diagram for Model Evaluation
items.summary: The target diagram is often used in geosciences, which provides a visualization tool for model evaluation and shows the temporal or spatial matching of data. However, its construction requires paired data of equal sample sizes, limiting its application to model comparisons involving unpaired samples or probability distributions. In this study, we propose the Wasserstein target diagram based on the 2-Wasserstein distance from optimal transport. Unlike the original target diagram, the Wasserstein target diagram does not require paired data of equal sizes and evaluates models from the probability distribution perspective. We further establish that the two target diagrams coincide when the given paired data are comonotone, which is common in climate science, such as cumulative precipitation and solar radiation. Through two simulation studies and an application to wind speed distribution fitting, we demonstrate that the proposed diagram can detect the probability distribution discrepancies that the original target diagram may not distinguish. The Wasserstein target diagram therefore lifts the model evaluation to the probability level and provides a complementary approach to estimating the agreement in probability distributions.

items.title: Semiparametric Efficient Inference under Non-Informative Complex Survey Designs
items.summary: Under non-informative complex survey designs, dependence among sampling indicators prevents the direct application of standard i.i.d. semiparametric efficiency theory. We introduce a \emph{reference Poisson experiment}, a hypothetical i.i.d.\ experiment constructed from the limiting inclusion probabilities of the original dependent design. Under suitable conditions, the actual observed-data experiment is in fact locally asymptotically normal, with the same tangent-space geometry as the reference Poisson experiment. Consequently, the efficient influence function derived by orthogonal projection in this hypothetical i.i.d.\ setting characterizes efficient estimators under the original dependent design. This yields a systematic approach to efficiency analysis for general semiparametric full-data models and pathwise-differentiable targets under complex survey designs. Under the joint superpopulation--design law, the efficiency bounds depend on the design only through its limiting inclusion probabilities. For finite-population targets whose first-order expansions are governed by the full-data efficient influence function, the same estimators are efficient under both superpopulation and finite-population centering, with bounds linked by a Pythagorean identity yielding a generalized finite-population correction. We establish efficiency of cross-fitted mean and conditional-mean regression estimators under explicit design-specific sufficient conditions. Simulations and California Academic Performance Index data illustrate the theory.

items.title: Adaptive Sparsity-Aware Projection-Assisted Spectral Embedding for High-Dimensional Noisy Data with Nonlinear Structures
items.summary: In this paper, we propose SPASE, an adaptive, sparsity-aware, projection-assisted spectral embedding method for feature extraction from high-dimensional noisy data with underlying nonlinear structures and latent sparsity patterns. We first construct a data-driven projection that adapts to the hidden sparsity patterns and the signal-to-noise ratio, reducing noise-induced distortion of pairwise distances. We then apply kernel-based spectral embedding to the projected data to explore the underlying geometric structure. The key methodological contribution is an energy-based projection selection algorithm that is adaptive to the signal-to-noise ratio and sparsity of the signal representation, while mitigating the impact of noise. On the theoretical side, we show that the resulting embeddings converge to the eigenfunctions of an integral operator associated with the latent signal, and the method can remain effective when the signal-to-noise ratio is low. We demonstrate the empirical performance of the proposed method through simulation studies and real-data applications, showing improved accuracy in downstream tasks such as classification and clustering.

items.title: Statistical Validation of Computer Models: Global and Subdomain Hypothesis Testing
items.summary: Computer simulations play an important role in scientific discovery and engineering innovation. Reliable computer models enable virtual experimentation that reduces the need for costly and time-consuming physical testing. However, the credibility of such models hinges on rigorous statistical validation against real-world data. This paper develops a formal frequentist framework for both global and subdomain validation of computer models. We propose the Fourier Maximum Modulus Test (FMMT), which leverages kernel ridge regression (KRR) to estimate the discrepancy between the computer model and the physical process, followed by a frequency-domain test based on weighted generalized Fourier coefficients. The theoretical analysis establishes the asymptotic normality of these coefficients, also when calibration parameters are estimated, allowing for closed-form p-values. Simulation studies and a shear-layer experiment demonstrate that FMMT achieves high power, accurate Type I error control, and strong sensitivity to localized discrepancies.

items.title: A Physically Informed Changepoint Score for Fault Prioritisation in District Heating
items.summary: Poorly cooling district-heating installations raise return temperatures and pumped flow, increasing heat losses and pumping energy and hindering low-temperature operation. Faults often go unreported for weeks, so their onset is unknown and energy is wasted in the meantime. Utilities flag poorly cooling installations by a low supply-return temperature difference, but not when the problem began. Changepoint detectors such as the Bayesian Estimator of Abrupt Change, Seasonality, and Trend (BEAST) can date a change but report only its probability, so a large, fault-like change and a marginal one can look alike. We therefore develop a decision score that weighs each BEAST change in temperature difference and flow by its probability, size, deviation from recent operation and physical direction. Joint falls in temperature difference and rises in flow, the signature of insufficient cooling, rank first. Across 1,522 cases, 648 with a reported fault, 24 of the 25 highest-ranked cases were reported faults, and Average Precision was 0.772 against a prevalence of 0.426, likely conservative, as unreported cases may contain faults. Without using the report date, the strongest flow rise in reported-fault cases came a median of 11 days before the report (128 days in comparison cases). Combined with temperature-difference screening, the score raised Average Precision in season-matched cases from 0.486 to 0.646. After the detected change, flagged reported-fault installations returned water 16 K warmer and about half their circulated water delivered no heat. The score gives utilities a short list for inspection and a candidate onset date for each change.

items.title: Minimax estimation for simultaneous deconvolution model in random design using wavelets
items.summary: Simultaneous deconvolution model is investigated when the design points are random and follow bounded densities and errors are either $i.i.d.$ or long-memory dependent. We propose wavelet hard-thresholding estimators, and show that they achieve asymptotically near-optimal convergence rates for the $L^2$-risk when the response function belongs to Besov space under both $i.i.d.$ errors and homoskedastic, long-memory errors. However, under heteroskedastic, long-memory errors the estimator is not optimal. For the $i.i.d.$ errors, the convergence rates are {identical} to those found in simultaneous deconvolution under regular design {and $i.i.d.$ errors}. However, for long-memory dependent errors, the convergence rates are new {and completely different from those in simultaneous deconvolution under regular design and long-memory errors}.

items.title: Bits, Not Boxes: Label-Free Layer Selection for Visual Localization in VLMs
items.summary: Attention maps cheaply show where a vision-language model (VLM) looks, but attention sinks make them unreliable for localization. Contrasting the question with a generic prompt suppresses sinks, yet only some layers localize the queried object. Existing methods find these layers with box annotations or fixed rules. We show that attention itself can identify them. A question changes how much a head attends to the image and where this attention goes. The two effects separate exactly, and the second, measured in bits on unlabeled questions, indicates which layers localize. WhereBits turns these where-to-look bits into a layer prior and combines it with per-head contrastive scores. Its three design constants were fixed once on labeled COCO data, and a new model or resolution needs only unlabeled questions. Across eight VLMs, WhereBits matches the pointing accuracy of box-tuned layers on COCO and RefCOCO and ranks target tokens better. This advantage holds on a held-out model family and at higher resolutions. Its COCO pointing accuracy is 0.72, against 0.22 for mean attention. In training-free zoom-in, its crops raise V* accuracy by 6.0 points under forced-choice evaluation.

items.title: Collaborative Optimal Design of Controlled Experiments with Subject Covariates
items.summary: Modern experimental design problems often encounter multiple controlled experiments with subjects participating in more than one experiment. It is of interest to consider the optimal design of allocating subjects to treatment or control for these experiments especially when subject covariate information is available. In this work, we propose an optimal allocation method to enable accurate estimates of treatment effects for all experiments. Deriving the precision matrix of the treatment effects and using D-optimality as our allocation criterion, we demonstrate the advantage of collaboratively designing and analyzing multiple experiments over traditional independent design and analysis, and propose efficient algorithms to design construction of the D-optimality problem for collaborative experiments. The performance of the proposed methods is examined by simulation studies and a case study involving online education experimentation.

items.title: The Spectral Distribution of Matrix Least Squares Solutions, and the Ellipsoid Fitting Problem
items.summary: We study the spectral distribution of the least squares solution to a random linear system whose unknown is a symmetric matrix. In the normalized and isotropic setting, we derive a closed-form description of the support of the spectral distribution. As an application, we consider the ellipsoid fitting problem: given $n$ standard Gaussian vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$, does there exist a centered ellipsoid passing through all of them? It was recently shown that this problem has a sharp phase transition at $n \approx d^2/4$. On the satisfiability side, unlike earlier results, these sharp results do not rely on least squares candidates. We show that the least squares candidates considered in earlier works have a threshold of positive semi-definiteness at $n \approx d^2/10$, which was previously observed numerically and predicted non-rigorously using statistical physics methods. Moreover, we show that the corresponding least squares dual certificates have a threshold of positive definiteness at $n \approx 2d^2/5$. Our approach combines several matrix concentration tools. A key technical ingredient, which may be of independent interest, is showing that a certain kernel matrix is well-conditioned with high probability until $n \approx d^2/2$.

items.title: When Does Subspace Direction Matter for LoRA? Regime Analysis of the Magnitude Principle in Few-Shot Adaptation
items.summary: We show that the importance of a LoRA adapter's initial input-subspace direction is regime-dependent, and we characterize this dependence in theory and experiment. This refines the recent view that spectral initializers help through update magnitude alone. Direction matters most when labeled data are scarce relative to the representation dimension and the activation subspace used for initialization captures supervised task structure. In this regime, the adapter's row span remains sensitive to its starting point, making task-aligned initialization especially useful. A spiked-covariance perturbation analysis characterizes the finite-sample stability of the estimated subspace. A first-step analysis of LoRA training explains why the subspace's alignment with the task matters and motivates an alignment coefficient $ρ$ that closely tracks gains across classification tasks. We test this account with PivotLoRA, which initializes adapters from activation PCA at prediction-relevant positions and applies one output-preserving orthogonal pivot early in training. In few-shot BERT-base classification, PivotLoRA achieves the best average rank among 13 methods and improves over vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings, even though it starts from a smaller input-factor initialization norm. Additional classification experiments extend the evaluation to 7B and 8B Llama decoders. Classification gains diminish with more labeled data, consistent with the proposed regime dependence. A targeted extension to completion-only reasoning also shows improvements on GSM8K and StrategyQA. These findings identify conditions under which initialization direction matters, with subspace-task alignment offering a low-cost diagnostic before training for classification.

items.title: Statistical Performance Guarantee for Subgroup Identification with Generic Machine Learning
items.summary: Across a wide array of disciplines, many researchers use machine learning (ML) algorithms to identify a subgroup of individuals who are likely to benefit from a treatment the most (``exceptional responders'') or those who are harmed by it. A common approach to this subgroup identification problem consists of two steps. First, researchers estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) using an ML algorithm. Next, they use the estimated CATE to select those individuals who are predicted to be most affected by the treatment, either positively or negatively. Unfortunately, CATE estimates are often biased and noisy. In addition, utilizing the same data to both identify a subgroup and estimate its group average treatment effect results in a multiple testing problem. To address these challenges, we develop uniform confidence bands for estimation of the group average treatment effect sorted by generic ML algorithm (GATES). Using these uniform confidence bands, researchers can identify, with a statistical guarantee, a subgroup whose GATES exceeds a certain effect size, regardless of how this effect size is chosen. The proposed methodology uses random treatment assignment, random sampling of units, and continuity and moment conditions, without requiring consistency or monotonicity of the ML score. We derive a Wiener representation of the estimation error, with corrections for the empirical subgroup threshold and the fixed treatment sample size. Estimating this representation gives asymptotically exact uniform coverage using Gaussian draws, without refitting the ML model. We also develop uniform bands for mean-adjusted treatment effects and other evaluation metrics. A simulation design and an application to a clinical trial of late-stage prostate cancer illustrate the subgroup identification problem.

items.title: LIC-Audit: How Comparable Are Reported Gains in Learned Image Compression?
items.summary: Learned image compression (LIC) papers often report BD-rate improvements of only a few percent. They are measured against VTM reference software whose version keeps changing: the claims we audit name 7 versions, 5 in 2025 papers alone. But how comparable are these numbers across papers, and what evidence should future papers give for such small gains? We introduce LIC-Audit, an analysis of 353 released rate-distortion curves from 36 repositories, and a controlled re-evaluation of eight public codec releases with 28,193 encode-decode records. We identify three problems. First, different VTM reference runs change BD-rates by up to 3.56 percentage points, and on CLIC Pro published numbers order 10 of 55 method pairs differently from a common computation; comparing codecs directly over a fixed quality range removes this dependence. Second, releases use different and mostly undocumented conventions for counting bits, computing PSNR, and padding images. Under consistent measurement, the GLIC method's 1.00% lead over the HPCM method on Tecnick becomes a 1.43% deficit, changing only the padding reverses the comparison of HPCM and CMIC, and most gaps narrow when MS-SSIM replaces PSNR. Third, average curves hide how much results vary from image to image, so whether a small gain is statistically significant depends on the assumed variation. An optimistic assumption calls 12.0% of comparisons between equally good codecs significant on test sets as small as Kodak, instead of 5%; a cautious one leaves 18 of 45 differences between recent codecs undecided, yet per-image results show 12 of them to be significant. Beyond auditing past results, LIC-Audit provides a versioned evaluation protocol, a public leaderboard website with a scoring tool, source-linked benchmark data, per-image measurements, and reporting guidelines, to help future LIC papers make comparable and verifiable claims of progress.

items.title: Inverse Design for Conditional Distribution Matching
items.summary: Generative models are powerful tools for sampling from a learned distribution $\mathcal{P}(Y \mid X)$, and inverse-design methods invert this map to find an input $x$ that produces a desired point output $y^*$. However, many design goals are naturally distributional rather than pointwise, incorporating the inherent uncertainty of $Y$ and targeting a specific form for it, a task not addressed by standard inverse design. To address this issue we introduce Conditional Distribution Matching (CDM), a new inverse-design problem class in generative modeling: given a joint distribution $\mathcal{P}(X, Y)$ and a target distribution $\mathcal{G}(Y)$, find an input $x^*$ whose induced conditional distribution $\mathcal{P}(Y \mid X = x^*)$ matches $\mathcal{G}$. We formally define two variants: Conditional Distribution Matching Sampling (CDMS) and Conditional Distribution Matching Optimization (CDMO). To solve these problems, we propose MLGD-F (Matching-Loss Guided Diffusion with a Fast inner sampler), a plug-and-play inference-time algorithm that combines a pretrained score-based diffusion model with a pretrained fast conditional sampler, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning. By leveraging single-step conditional sampling, MLGD-F enables tractable gradient computation, making the estimation of $\mathcal{P}(Y \mid X)$ both memory-efficient and computationally lightweight. We validate MLGD-F on synthetic benchmarks, structured image transformations, and generative editing optimization, demonstrating reliable recovery of inputs whose conditional distributions match diverse user-specified targets, including discrete mixtures and continuous low-rank supports.

items.title: Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives
items.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. This bias induces a reverse learning order, in which sequence-level OPD first matches the teacher at later token positions, while at earlier positions it can favor tokens that are improbable under the teacher, and thus often undesirable. As for the choice of divergence, we prove that it strongly influences the amenability of OPD to gradient-based optimization. In particular, while the forward KL divergence enjoys a well-behaved objective landscape, other $f$-divergences, such as reverse KL, can suffer from vanishing gradients even when the student and teacher are far apart. Across language model post-training settings, we demonstrate the implications of these theoretical findings for which OPD objective is preferable, highlighting the importance of accounting for the interplay between the student, teacher, and task at hand.

items.title: Fold Weighting for Cross-Validation Under Continuous Distributional Drift
items.summary: Cross-validation weights all folds equally, so under drift the oldest folds count as much as the newest. We model drift by a Hölder condition in total variation distance and give finite-sample bounds on the excess deployment risk of the configuration that sliding-window cross-validation selects. Each bound splits into drift, estimation, and validation-noise terms. With equal weights the drift terms saturate as the record grows. With fold weights fixed in advance, the drift terms become weighted averages, which shrink as weight moves toward deployment. The noise term grows as the weights concentrate and shrinks with the batch size. The drift terms are linear in the weights and the noise term is convex, so minimizing the bound over the weights is a convex problem. Applications to U.S. earnings and flight delays show both sides of this trade-off. Weight on recent folds pays off when a change in the best predictor persists and each period has many observations, and equal weights do best when changes are short-lived.

items.title: Inference after coding agents
items.summary: Empirical research is changing rapidly as AI coding agents are becoming increasingly proficient in every step of it, from writing code to manipulating data. We argue that while the potential of coding agents for science is vast, their use in hypothesis testing poses a substantial threat to classical inference, as these agents enable a supercharged form of selective inference. In particular, we argue that coding agents carrying out empirical research introduce a new type of post-selection inference that combines human-like, open-ended search over an implicit space of estimators with programmatic replayability of both the selection and the estimation process. Indeed, we find that on simulated data with zero effects, four frontier agents report significant p-values between 54% and 98% of the time when asked to produce a compelling finding. We propose a simple procedure for detecting and correcting these distortions. After an agent has completed its analysis, we reset and replay it on subsamples of the data to estimate the agent's relative probability of selecting that analysis when it looks statistically favorable. For agents with stable selection behavior, the resulting corrected test is asymptotically valid and consistent conditional on selection. Importantly, the correction is learned from the black-box agent's actual choices rather than a model of how it searches, so it remains valid even as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly. In simulations, the correction robustly lowers the high false rejection rates to near the nominal 5%. We illustrate the method on applications from two published papers.

items.title: Generative sequence modeling for infinite memory processes via predictive states
items.summary: We consider estimating the one-step-ahead conditional distribution of a multivariate stochastic process. Many existing approaches rely on structural assumptions such as finite-range memory, sparsity, or additivity, which can be poorly suited to processes with long-range nonlinear interactions. However, without such structural assumptions, nonparametric estimation is known to be challenging due to the curse of dimensionality. To address this challenge, we introduce a new estimator based on the idea of learning representations of the \emph{predictive states} of a stochastic process. We theoretically analyze several aspects of this problem. As a bonus, we establish convergence rate guarantees for an instantiation of our method based on deep neural network estimators. Our results suggest that faster convergence rates are achievable when the predictive state space is lower-dimensional. That is, when the past history can be compressed into a lower-dimensional statistic that is sufficient for predicting the future. We implement our method in PyTorch and evaluate its performance on synthetic data and real \emph{C. elegans} data.

items.title: Inference for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Deep Survival Learners
items.summary: Conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) provide a principled framework for assessing treatment-effect heterogeneity and identifying patients who may benefit from an intervention. For survival outcomes, CATEs may also evolve over time and pose challenges for estimation and inference. Existing methods can accommodate complex covariate heterogeneity but often fail to exploit shared temporal structure or provide valid inference for time-varying treatment effects and their contrasts. We propose a deep survival learning framework that combines neural networks for nonparametric covariate effects with a shared spline representation of temporal variation, enabling joint estimation of CATE trajectories. Using doubly robust pseudo-outcomes and sample splitting, we establish nonasymptotic oracle bounds accounting for network and temporal approximation, nuisance estimation, and optimization errors. Our theory shows that exploiting shared temporal structure yields sharper error bounds for temporal contrasts than those derived from separate time-specific estimators. For inference, we develop a subsampled ensemble procedure and establish asymptotic normality for pointwise CATEs, temporal contrasts, and covariate contrasts, including temporal contrasts over shrinking time intervals. Under suitable regularity and bias-control conditions, consistent infinitesimal jackknife variance estimators yield asymptotically valid confidence intervals. Simulations evaluate estimation accuracy, interval coverage, and sensitivity to temporal dimension and basis mismatch. An application to lung cancer survival data illustrates the framework's ability to characterize heterogeneous treatment benefits over time.

items.title: Amortizing Tempered Sampling with Corrected Self-Training
items.summary: Learning a neural sampler can reduce the cost of repeated sampling from an un-normalized distribution, but obtaining good training data remains difficult. We develop a corrected self-training scheme across a sequence of tempered targets, making use of importance sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo to correct the samples and replay buffers to store them. We introduce Sequential Score Sampler (SSS) as a particular case. In SSS, the proposal is a score-based diffusion trained by regression on energy gradients; and the samples are corrected by importance weights on the path space. After training, samples can be collected directly from the model, from its importance-corrected proposals, or from the final-temperature buffer. The method amortizes repeated sampling by encoding the global structure of the target in the model. SSS achieves competitive sampling accuracy across the benchmarks and, on several targets, uses shorter runtimes with fewer energy evaluations than competing samplers.

items.title: PRESCCO: Efficient Prediction Intervals under a Right-Censored Covariate
items.summary: In neurodegenerative diseases, atypical patients can reveal disease-modifying biology. A patient is atypical when their outcome falls outside a prediction interval for patients at the same point in the disease, measured by the time to a disease event. Most patients leave the study before the event, so their time to it is right-censored, and no method computes a prediction interval with a right-censored covariate. We develop the first methods. We adapt three conformal prediction methods and show that their estimated half-length, half the interval's width, varies across studies, changing which patients are identified as atypical. We then develop the PRESCCO method. We prove its estimator of the half-length is doubly robust, consistent when one of its time-to-event and censoring models is misspecified, and semiparametrically efficient when both are correct. At a 90% prediction level, its prediction interval identifies close to 10% of patients as atypical, across studies and, with high probability, in a single study. In simulations, its estimated half-length is four to thirty times less variable than under conformal prediction. In Huntington disease data with 77.2% right-censoring, the PRESCCO method identifies close to the targeted 10% of patients as atypical, whereas conformal prediction identifies too many or too few.

items.title: Milk yield responses to heat stress in tropical dairy cattle
items.summary: Context: Rising temperatures and warm tropical nights threaten dairy productivity and resilience across tropical landscapes. Objective: This study characterises multi-scale interactions among thermal regimes, nighttime cooling, metabolic heat load, and crossbred genetics on daily milk yield in Brazilian dairy systems. Methods: A 24-year panel (2001--2024) of 788,528 test-day records from 87,809 Girolando (Holstein $\times$ Gyr) cows across 408 municipalities was linked to weather data. Two-way fixed effects, distributed lag, and piecewise threshold spline models were estimated across yield quartiles and crossbred fractions. Results: While aggregate summaries suggest stable yield up to a daily mean Temperature--Humidity Index (THI) of 76, production-stratified splines show high-yielding cows lose milk starting at THI 68 and accelerating above 76 ($-0.162$ kg animal$^{-1}$ d$^{-1}$ unit$^{-1}$, $p=0.0062$), whereas low-yielding cows remain unaffected ($p=0.81$). Distributed lag models reveal an immediate drop followed by a deeper trough four days later. Lack of nighttime relief ($\mathrm{THI}_{\min} \ge 68$) reduces yield by an extra 2.37 kg animal$^{-1}$ d$^{-1}$ ($p \le 0.001$) and causes an 8.6\% loss after seven warm nights, whereas wide diurnal amplitude buffers output by $+1.60$ kg animal$^{-1}$ d$^{-1}$. At comparable high yields ($\approx 31$ kg animal$^{-1}$ d$^{-1}$), intermediate crossbreds ($1/2$ and $5/8$ Holstein) sustain yield up to THI 76, whereas $7/8$ Holstein cows decline at THI 68. Conclusions: Tropical dairy adaptation requires continuous nighttime cooling for high-yielding cows combined with balanced Zebu--taurine crossbreeding.
authors: Marcos Vinicius Gualberto Barbosa da Silva

items.title: Symmetries of Counterfactuals: Identification and Testability of Counterfactual Maps from Covariate Heterogeneity
items.summary: In general, counterfactuals are not identified from data alone, because many causal models produce the same observed distributions but different counterfactuals. A common approach to circumvent this problem is to restrict the mechanism to a class in which it becomes unique, such as triangular monotone maps or optimal transport maps. However, whether the assumed class is correct is usually not examined. In this work, we study what the data can tell us when covariates are available that influence the outcome only through its latent cause. First, we characterise all counterfactual maps that are consistent with the data. They differ from the true map by a group of symmetries that preserve the conditional outcome distributions given the covariates. The more these distributions vary across covariate values, the smaller the group. Second, we show that for the classes above, consistency with the data is equivalent to a single conditional independence, which yields a test of the assumed class. We illustrate both results on synthetic data and on the ACTG 175 HIV trial.

items.title: JALE: A new Python toolbox for coordinate-based neuroimaging meta-analysis using activation likelihood estimation
items.summary: Coordinate-based neuroimaging meta-analysis using activation likelihood estimation (ALE) is commonly used to synthesize reported results of functional or structural magnetic resonance imaging studies. We here present JALE, a new, open-source Python package for conducting ALE meta-analyses. Besides computing standard ALE main effects and contrast analyses, this toolbox implements several novel analytical approaches including new options for thresholding (threshold-free cluster enhancement statistics, significance threshold prediction) as well as sensitivity and cluster analyses that were only available as in-house scripts in the past. The purpose of this paper is to provide an integrated conceptual foundation of recent developments in the ALE meta-analysis framework, with a particular focus on novel methodological implementations that can be executed in a straightforward and standardized manner using the new JALE toolbox.

items.title: Action-outcome coupling: a pre-investment feasibility audit for offline reinforcement learning in supply chain operations
